text: {"answer": "The passages suggest the answer depends on baseline vitamin D status. Supplementation reliably corrects deficiency and improves measured bone mineral density in adults with low serum levels, supporting daily use in that group [vitamin_d#0]. Deficient populations also show better muscle strength and fewer falls after daily supplementation [vitamin_d#3]. A meta-analysis reports a modest fracture benefit in older adults when vitamin D is combined with calcium over sustained daily use [vitamin_d#1]. The contrary evidence is substantial: a Cochrane review found no reduction in all-cause mortality in adults who are not deficient at baseline [vitamin_d#5], the VITAL trial of about 25,000 participants found no significant effect on cardiovascular events or cancer [vitamin_d#4], and routine supplementation with adequate serum levels showed no measurable outcome improvement and added cost and pill burden [vitamin_d#6]. High doses have been linked to hypercalcaemia and, in some trials, to increased fall risk in older adults [vitamin_d#7]. Observational links to immune benefit are associational only [vitamin_d#2].
